summary: A travel-essay style note collecting humorous stories about ancestral spirits and totems told by storytellers from many Indigenous communities between September 2023 and January 2024. Each tale shows a revered figure such as Raven, Coyote, Maui, Bear or the Kamuy in a comic mishap. The note concludes that laughter is a sacred medicine that heals and connects communities.
one_line: A whimsical tour of humorous Indigenous totem and ancestral spirit tales gathered from storytellers across several regions in 2023-2024.
key_facts: On September 5, 2023, at the Neechee festival in Thunder Bay, elder Joseph "Laughing Otter" McKay told how the trickster totem Raven was outfoxed by a cunning squirrel.
On September 20, 2023, in the Navajo Nation, storyteller Sarah "Twinkling Star" Yazzie told of Coyote mistaking a cactus for a potential mate after a rain dance.
On October 12, 2023, Hemi "Kea's Cackle" Te Kahu of the Maori Iwi of Aotearoa narrated how the demigod Maui tried to transform into various creatures with his magical fishhook.
Maui's transformations in Hemi Te Kahu's tale never mastered the intended totem shape but entertained his brother and sister deities.
On October 25, 2023, at a Haida gathering, Margaret "Mirthful Mink" Wilson told of the Bear, a symbol of strength and leadership, struggling with slippery salmon during the great fish run.
On November 8, 2023, in the Amazon, Yanomami shaman Carlos "Chuckling Toucan" Pereira told of a forest spirit who made a bow from a living vine that entangled him in knots.
On December 15, 2023, Kwakwaka'wakw elder Kathryn "Hooting Owl" Johnson described carvings on totem poles depicting each creature's comical mishap.
In Kathryn Johnson's description, a Beaver at the bottom of a totem pole has a tail bitten by his own teeth, while the Eagle at the top looks bashful after mistaking a rock for prey.
On January 10, 2024, beside a bonfire among the Ainu of Japan, Akira "Grinning Bear" Suzuki told how the Kamuy (gods) tripped over their divine robes during sacred rituals.
The note concludes that indigenous cultures understand the power of humor and that laughter is a sacred medicine capable of healing and connecting communities.
The Raven is described in the note as a renowned trickster totem, and Coyote as often seen as a wise ancestral spirit.
